chunks: "The input capacitor is part of the hot loop with the high-side and low-side switches, so I route it first and treat its connection as an inductance problem.
It goes right against the VIN and power-ground pins of the IC, on the same layer, with short, wide copper straight from the capacitor pads to the pins, and no vias between the capacitor and the pins.
If the capacitor's ground side goes to the plane, the via goes right at the capacitor's ground pad so the return current drops straight into the plane under the loop.
I use a small ceramic, something like 0.

1 to 1 microfarads in 0402 or 0603, closest to the pins, because it has the lowest ESL and highest self-resonant frequency, and then a larger ceramic, say 10 microfarads, next to it, and a bulk capacitor further away to handle the lower frequencies and damp the source.
If the IC has several VIN/PGND pin pairs, I place a capacitor at each.
And I like the input power to flow through the capacitor pads before it reaches the IC, so the capacitor isn't on a stub.
I check the effective capacitance at the DC bias, because a 10 microfarads 25 volts ceramic can lose half at 12 volts.
The reason is that a few nanohenries in this loop gives volts of overshoot and ringing: a 5 amps pulse in 3 nanoseconds across 3 nanohenries is 5 volts."
